introduction.p: The midpoint rule uses a rectangle whose height is the function value at the midpoint. The trapezoidal rule joins the endpoint values by a line. Applying either rule on many subintervals approximates an integral. We will derive their error bounds under bounds on the second derivative.

subsection.p: Why use the midpoint instead of an endpoint? The midpoint balances the interval. If the function is increasing, a left rectangle underestimates and a right rectangle overestimates. The midpoint often cancels part of those errors.
For a line, the cancellation is perfect.

exercise.title: Why is a midpoint rectangle often better than a left or right one?

statement.p: On one interval, the midpoint rule uses height f\bigl((a+b)/2\bigr). In your own words, why does that choice often cancel part of the error of endpoint rectangles, and why is the rule exact for every line?

hint.p: If a function is increasing, a left rectangle underestimates and a right rectangle overestimates. The midpoint height of a line is exactly its average height.

example.title: midpoint rule is exact for a line
example.p: So the midpoint rule gives the exact answer.
This happens for every linear function on every interval. The midpoint height of a line is exactly the average height of the line.

subsection.title: Error patterns from concavity
subsection.p: The trapezoidal rule replaces the graph by a secant line. The midpoint rule replaces the graph by a horizontal line at the midpoint height.
Concavity tells us which approximation lies above or below the true area.
If
on an interval, the graph is concave up. It bends upward. The secant line lies above the graph, so the trapezoid overestimates the integral.
For the same concave-up graph, the midpoint rectangle underestimates the integral. The curve spends more area above the midpoint height than below it.

exercise.title: How does concavity decide overestimate versus underestimate?

statement.p: Suppose f'' does not change sign on [a,b]. In your own words, why does a concave-up graph make the trapezoidal rule overestimate and the midpoint rule underestimate, and why can that pattern fail if concavity changes?

hint.p: A secant lies above a concave-up graph. The midpoint rectangle sits at a height that, for the same shape, leaves more area above it than below. Changing concavity mixes the two pictures.

subsection.title: Error bounds
subsection.p: An error pattern tells us the direction of the error. An error bound tells us how large the error can be.

The size of the error is controlled by curvature. If the graph is nearly linear on each small interval, the midpoint and trapezoidal rules are accurate. The second derivative measures how far the graph is from being linear.

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: On a subinterval [c,d], let L be the line through the endpoint values. For an interior point x, choose C so that f(t)-L(t)-C(t-c)(t-d) vanishes at c,x,d. warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A numerical rule may still produce numbers when its error-bound hypotheses fail.
The formula for the guarantee is what fails, not necessarily the approximation itself.

paragraphs.p: This warning matters in applications. Before using an error bound, check the interval, the continuity of the derivatives, and whether the integral is proper.
The midpoint and trapezoidal rules approximate a curve by flat or straight pieces. The next rule asks a natural question:

p.me: \text{What if we approximate the graph by a parabola instead?}

paragraphs.p: That idea leads to Simpson’s Rule.

exercise.title: What does an error bound guarantee, and when does the formula fail?

statement.p: The midpoint and trapezoidal bounds shrink like 1/n^2 and are controlled by a bound on |f''|. In your own words, why is a bound not a prediction of the exact error, and why can the rules still be used on \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx even though those particular bounds do not apply?

hint.p: Curvature measures how far the graph is from linear. If f'' is unbounded, the guarantee fails. The approximation itself may still produce useful numbers.
